caps.text: Module 1, Lesson 1. Clean a messy ledger in 10 minutes.
It's the first working day of April.
Kopi Mesra, a two-outlet café, has just sent you their March
ledger export.
101 rows. Vendor names spelled three different ways. Blank
account codes. And somewhere in there, a few transactions
posted twice.
Cleaning this by hand could take you an afternoon.
In this lesson, we'll do it with Claude in about 10 minutes, and
we'll check every number along the way.
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to do three things.
Upload a ledger and get a clear list of issues, without Claude
changing anything yet.
Check Claude's findings by tying out the totals.
And ask for a clean, categorised file you can review and use.
Step one. Prepare the file safely.
Before you upload anything, check your firm's policy on using
AI tools.
Remove anything you don't need, like customer names, IC numbers,
or bank account numbers.
For this course, you'll use the Kopi Mesra practice file. It's a
fictional company, so it's safe to upload.
Download it from the lesson resources. It's called M1 ledger
March messy.
Step two. Upload the file and give Claude a clear
first instruction.
Open Claude, attach the spreadsheet, and type a prompt
like this.
First, the background: who you are, and what the file is.
Then the request: find the problems, and name the kinds of
problems you care about.
And one important rule: don't change anything yet. We want a
list first, so we stay in control.
Now look at the last part. We ask for the totals, and for
anything Claude is unsure about. That's the fact-check habit,
and you'll use it in every lesson.
Step three. Read the issues list.
Here's the summary you should get from the practice file. These
are the issues we planted for you to find.
Six possible duplicates, worth RM 7,133.13.
Fourteen rows with no account code.
Three payments with no reference number.
Twenty-five different spellings for just thirteen vendors.
And two unusual items: a RM 5,000 cash withdrawal on a Sunday,
posted to suspense, and a home air fryer that may be a
personal expense.
Claude's wording will be different from this, and that's fine.
What matters is that you check it.
Step four. Tie out the totals. Never skip this.
Total debits in the original file: RM 126,078.67.
Take out the six duplicates, and debits drop to RM 118,945.54.
The difference is exactly RM 7,133.13, the value of the
duplicates. The numbers agree.
But before you remove anything, check each duplicate against the
source document. Two identical rows aren't always a mistake.
Sometimes there really were two deliveries.
Step five. Ask for the clean file.
Once you've checked the list, reply with clear rules, like this.
Use only accounts from the chart of accounts. Standardise the
vendor names. Flag duplicates instead of deleting them. And
don't change any amounts.
You get back a cleaned spreadsheet, with a standard vendor name,
a suggested account, and a status for every row.
Anything Claude isn't sure about is marked for review, so you
make the final call.
Let's recap.
Prepare your file safely. Ask for an issues list first. Tie out
the totals. Then ask for the clean file, with clear rules.
Now it's your turn. Download the practice file, run both
prompts, and fill in the tie-out sheet in Workbook 1.
Remember: Claude does the heavy lifting, but you're the
accountant. You sign off on the numbers.
In the next lesson, you'll learn the BRIEF method: a simple way
to write prompts that work every time.
